chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 341 to 360: short akam poems of waiting and leaving, in which the friend and the foster mother weigh the road (343, 347, 356), the mullai season and the evening return as signs (344, 352, 358), the veri rite and night visits endanger the secret love (355, 360), marriage silences the gossip (351), and a given beauty cannot be asked back (349).

341.reading: The woman tells her friend that even in this season when the kuravam is spread with many blossoms and the punku with its puffed-rice flowers adorns the grove, though her lover does not cherish her, she will make her unwilling heart firm, telling it that the manly purpose great men set their hearts on is not to be faulted, and so live on by her own hardness.
341.nuance: She answers her own grief with the man's own argument: the great are right to pursue their manly work (ஆண்மை), so she will not blame it, and she calls the strength that lets her survive her வன்கண், a word for cruelty or hardness, as if enduring were itself a fault. The colophon's neythal has nothing in the poem to support it: the flowers are of the spring, the season of paalai.

thinai_evidence.note: she steels herself to bear his going in the flowering season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 7 names the friend as addressee

342.reading: The friend asks the man of the hill country, where the forest-dweller who forgot to guard the big fragrant-segmented jackfruit a male monkey has already handled now sets snares on every guarded tree, whether it is fitting that this girl suffers here over the cool kuvalai leaf-skirt he gave, if he is one whose nature never comes to the point of relieving the distress of those who love him.
342.nuance: The leaf-skirt was a lover's gift; the friend makes it the cause of the girl's suffering, since the household has noticed it. The snares set after the fruit is touched read as the guard that comes too late, which is the household watch that now keeps the girl in.

thinai_evidence.note: hill things and the hill lord frame a friend's demand

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative குன்ற நாட names the man; the friend presses him over the girl's suffering

ullurai.tenor: the man who has already won the girl and the household that now guards her too late

pairs.situation: the man has already touched the girl in secret
the household was careless while the secret love began
now the household guards her closely, so meetings are barred

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses things of the hill, the land of this kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

343.reading: The friend asks the girl to think about the road that leaves with the man of the high hills, a road where a mighty tiger with gaping mouth that leapt at the adorned face of a tusker with musth-wet cheeks lies, its white teeth stained red, on the drooping flowered branch of a black-trunked vengai bent by the west wind at the mouth of a cleft.
343.nuance: The tiger has fought and now rests, its prey not named as killed; the road is dangerous, but the danger lies spent on a flowering branch, and the friend may be telling the girl that with this man even such a road can be taken. Whether she urges the journey or warns against it turns on நினையாய், which can be 'consider it' or 'you do not consider'.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend proposes that the girl leave with the man

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 1 is the friend's address to the girl as companion

344.reading: The woman tells her friend that those who see their lovers come back, lovers who left in pursuit of rare wealth, must surely have done penance, in this cold harsh month of blown spray, in the sad evening when the cows with swollen udders, having grazed the field crops with the great bull, drip milk thinking of their calves, leave the herd and head for the village.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits through the cold evening for the man away for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 1 names the friend

iraicchi.act: the cows, udders dripping, leave the herd at evening to go home to their calves
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle go home at evening to those who need them, but he stays away for wealth

345.reading: The friend asks the man whether it would be a fault if he halted his tall chariot with its ornaments and curved seat on the long sand that looks like a hill and rested and stayed, so that the loneliness of this girl with the drooping leaf-skirt might leave her, at their small good town fenced by the great water, where the curving backwater with its shining waves, laced with thazhai, roars.
345.nuance: The invitation is phrased as a question about blame (தவறோ), so it is the friend who takes the risk of asking; her loneliness (புலம்பு) is to end by his staying in the town, not by a night tryst.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-shore town by the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the plural address தங்கினிர் and the chariot name the man as addressee

346.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man of the land where a young tusker with budding tusks, desiring a young she-elephant, comes near the hill and, while the hill people shout, cuts across the village common, came in the morning bringing a garland of spring kuvalai, chased the parrots by the millet field, and at evening, longing for her, wearied and shrank away unable even to speak.
346.nuance: The bold elephant that cuts through the common in spite of the shouting is set against the man who, having come with gifts and served at the millet field, cannot get a word out: the friend's picture of his boldness outside and helplessness before her is a plea that the girl take pity.

thinai_evidence.note: hill folk, the millet field and the hill elephant

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 3 is the friend's address to the girl

ullurai.tenor: the young man who wants the girl and comes into the village despite its talk

pairs.situation: the young man who desires the girl
the villagers' noise and talk around him
he still comes openly into the village to see her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the hill elephant and hill folk of this kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

347.reading: The man tells his heart that if she has made one union with them on the long forest road at the edge of the wasteland where the full springs have dried, where the fragrant flowers of the young vaakai on their stalks look like the crest of a young dark peacock, then good is the resolve it desired.
347.nuance: The road is dry, yet he sees in it a flower like a peacock's crest: with her beside him, the waste already looks adorned. ஒன்றுமணம், a union that makes them one, is the elopement read as a marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: he weighs taking the girl with him across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the vaakai flowers on their stalks

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the hero speaks to his own heart (நெஞ்சம், line 6)

348.reading: The friend asks the girl whether, if they go off by themselves, the man will not see her tears, which, like the small mullai flowers caught on the tusks of an elephant searching the land in the forest and scattered with crushed petals, flow and wet her lovely breasts with their ornaments.
348.nuance: The simile takes the flowers from the elephant of the road he will travel, so the tears are pictured with the very road that causes them; the question 'will he not see' hopes that her weeping will stop his going.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave on the forest road

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative மாணிழை in line 6 names the girl

349.reading: The woman tells her friend, who says they should take back their beauty from the lord of the cool shore where on the sand dune sits the big-legged stork that tears the lovely opened adumbu flowers and eats fish, that they could take it, but would losing their dear life be more painful than saying 'give back what was given' to those who, fearing hardship, begged and received.
349.nuance: She grants the friend's claim and refuses it: a gift cannot be asked back, so her beauty, once given, is his even if she dies of it. The giver's code of the puram poets becomes the measure of a lover's dignity.

thinai_evidence.note: the stork and the sand dune of the shore

comparisons.tenor: demanding her beauty back from the man

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 4 names the friend, whose proposal the woman answers

ullurai.tenor: the man who spoiled her beauty for his pleasure and now sits at ease

pairs.situation: he took his pleasure of her
he now rests at ease on his shore, unmoved

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the stork and creeper of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

350.reading: The friend says to the woman: had they stood before him and said 'we cannot bear the cold harsh season, do not go', would he have gone, the one who left in the grip of unstable wealth across the hilly forest where the long-legged lapwing with dark blades of wings sits by the path and, by sensing men, makes the travellers turn their weapons forward.
350.nuance: The friend blames their own silence, not his going: had they spoken he would have stayed. நிலையாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, is the ethicists' phrase, here turned into the argument that he gave up what lasts for what does not. The bird's part in lines 5 and 6 is uncertain: it may warn travellers of robbers or warn robbers of travellers.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the address அம்ம வாழி தோழி in line 1 is the friend's opening to the woman

351.reading: The friend tells the bangled girl to rejoice: their people have declared the right to the lord of the shore where the thunder-voiced waves break with a roar, ruining the wet sand path the swift crooked-legged crab that lives in holes had striped with its sharp claws; and she asks whether this gossiping town, with the sweet-smiling girls of the fish-smelling quarter where blossoming punnai rise, is still the same.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore, the crab, the punnai and the fishing quarter

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative வளையோய் in line 1 names the girl

ullurai.tenor: the secret love and its traces, erased by the public declaration of marriage

pairs.situation: the marks of the lovers' secret meetings that set the town talking
the kin's loud public declaration of the marriage
the trail of gossip is wiped out

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the crab and the surf of the shore, the land of this neythal poem (porul 7.27)

352.reading: The woman tells her friend that she learned the reality of the small dull evening, when the sharp-clawed creature with curved soft wings like the back of a long-stemmed water-lily leaf heads for the slope of broad-leaved jackfruit, leaving lonely the old tree where it rested by day, only after she stopped seeing him.
352.nuance: The colophon files it under paalai; the poem has no road and no waste, only the evening hour and a woman who waits, so it is read here by its hour and its situation.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening hour of a waiting woman

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 6 names the friend

iraicchi.act: the bat leaves the old tree where it rested by day, leaving it lonely, and flies off to the jackfruit slope
iraicchi.sense: as the bat abandons its day-tree at evening, so he left her, and she is the tree left lonely

353.reading: The friend says that by day, bathing in the resounding waterfall on the slope of the tall-peaked hill with the noisy hill lord's chest as a raft is sweet, but at night, in the good house with the red flame of a white cotton wick, with eyes whose lined lids will not close, to sleep while mother embraces the small back where the braids fall is bitter.
353.nuance: Day and night are set side by side: the daytime meeting is sweet, but the nights under the mother's guarding embrace are sleepless, so day meetings are no longer enough and he must marry her. The mother's embrace, a comfort, is felt as a guard.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, its waterfall and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the hill lord's chest, held while bathing

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no vocative; read as the friend speaking within the man's hearing to urge marriage

354.reading: The friend tells the man that if one bathes too long even the eyes turn red and in the mouth of the sated even honey turns sour; if he has grown distant, let him take them back to their house, them whom he once freed from trembling fear and distress in the street where fierce snakes move in their father's town of the cool pond.
354.nuance: Two maxims of satiety open the poem, and the friend lets them stand as the explanation of his coldness without accusing him; then she reminds him he was once the one who brought the girl out of fear, so returning her home would undo his own rescue.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's estrangement

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the second-person தணந்தனை names the man

355.reading: The friend asks the lord of the tall hill how he came in the dead of a night when many sleep, when rain blinds the eyes so the sky cannot be seen, water spreads and flows so the ground cannot be seen, and day has gone so the dark is deep, and how he found their small hamlet where the vengai is fragrant; and she says she grieves.
355.nuance: Three clauses each take away a way of seeing (sky, ground, light), so the question 'how did you come' is fear for him, and under it a hint that such nights should end in marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: the midnight tryst in the hill hamlet

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative ஓங்கல் வெற்ப in line 5 names the man

356.reading: The foster mother wonders how she will manage, the girl like a tender shoot with small shapely bangles, who would not drink the milk mixed with fine puffed rice held up in a fashioned vessel of red gold, saying it was too much, now that, guarded by the anklet-wearing man, she hurries through the hard waterless way where the shade has died, and by a dried-up spring must gulp the scalding muddy water.
356.nuance: The contrast is all in the mouth: milk in a gold bowl refused at home, scalding mud gulped on the road. The man appears only as the anklet-wearer who guards her, so the mother's grief is not against him but for the child's body.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has left with the man across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

357.reading: The friend says that before the lord of the sky-touching hill, where the tall fine elephant that turned back from the firebrand of the watchman guarding the small millet fears even the gleam of lightning, came to unite with her, her shoulders were rounded and always earned the word 'good'; now her collyrium-lined eyes, sleepless and labouring in hateful grief, run with tears, and her shoulders, their beauty bowed, have grown thin and slip.
357.nuance: The elephant scared once by the watchman's firebrand that now fears even lightning may hint at a man made timid by the household's watch, who no longer comes; but the poem draws no pair beyond one mood, so it stays scene. The syntax of lines 1 to 4 is hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, its watchman and the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

358.reading: The friend tells the woman, who sobs here with her heavy bangles slipping, bewildered, her darting eyes, scoring lines and clinging to the wall, that the season he promised, saying he would come so that her distant grief would end, is there to see: in the cold evening when the lonely grieve, the white buds of the mullai are like the cowherds' garlands, as if they spoke it.
358.nuance: The scoring of lines on the wall is the counting of days, and the friend answers it with a sign outside the wall: the buds are the promise kept by the season, so he must be near. Line 7 was repaired from Swaminatha Aiyar's text and its syntax remains hard.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai buds and the herdsmen of the rainy evening

comparisons.tenor: the white mullai buds announcing the season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the second-person நின் and உதுக்காண் name the woman

359.reading: The friend tells the bard to see how seemly it is: in the evening under the spreading fresh white moonlight, on the short-legged cot with its fragrant flower bed, the man, breathing like an elephant at rest, longingly embraced his son, and the son's mother embraced the victorious man's back.
359.nuance: No one embraces the other directly: the father holds the son and the mother holds the father from behind, so the child closes the circle. Told to the bard, the go-between of the man's other loves, the scene also says his office is no longer needed.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard's errand ends in the family's own embrace

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative பாண in line 1 names the bard

360.reading: The woman tells her friend that even if today they must bear the grievous pining because their mother sees that the velan, taking it for possession, does not know the cure for the sickness, may he not come at night, the lord of the shining hill with groves that echo on the slopes, where the rattle in the hill girl's hand scares off the parrots eating the big-eared millet like a she-elephant's trunk.
360.nuance: She would rather suffer the mistaken rite at home than have him risk the night path: the veri rite misreads her sickness, and the one true cure she forbids for his sake.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, the hill girl and the hill lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி in line 4 names the friend

links.note: In Akananuru 54 the returning man sees the milch herd hurrying home at dusk to the calves with the cowherds behind and wants to reach his wife and son; in Kuruntokai 344 the waiting woman sees the cows with dripping udders leave the herd for the village at dusk and says only the fortunate see their lovers return.
links.teaches: The same dusk image of cows hurrying home to their calves is the man's cue to return when he speaks and the woman's reproach when she speaks, so the herd's homing is a fixed sign of the duty to come home that each side reads against the other.

links.note: In Akananuru 110 a stranger asks the bathing girls if he may eat with them and stay in their noisy fishing hamlet, and they turn him away; in Kuruntokai 345 the friend herself asks the man whether staying with his chariot at their small town by the great water would be a fault.
links.teaches: The night's stay in the fishing hamlet is the neythal courtship's measure of trust: asked for by the stranger at the start and refused, it is offered by the friend once the love is known, so who proposes the stay marks how far the affair has gone.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 236 the friend tells the lord of the shore to give back the beauty he consumed before he leaves; in Kuruntokai 349 the woman answers such a proposal by saying that demanding back what was given is worse than losing one's life.
links.teaches: The demand to return her beauty, which the friend can make as a just claim, the woman herself refuses because it treats her love as a loan, so the same claim is fair in a friend's mouth and shameful in the giver's, by the code that a gift is not taken back.

links.note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so whoever gets it should at once do what lasts; in Kuruntokai 350 the friend calls the wealth for which the man left நிலையாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, and regrets they did not stop him.
links.teaches: The ethicist's premise that wealth does not stay becomes in akam an argument against the journey itself: the Kural spends unstable wealth on lasting good, while the friend counts the lasting thing given up as the woman's company, so the same premise judges the pursuit of wealth from the household's side.

links.note: In Kural 1150 the friend tells the woman the town raises the very gossip they want, since the lover will grant marriage when asked; in Kuruntokai 351 the friend tells the girl to rejoice because their kin have declared the marriage, and asks whether the gossiping town is still the same.
links.teaches: The couplet hopes the town's gossip will force the marriage, and the poem shows the end of that hope: once the kin declare the marriage, the talk that pressed for it has nothing left to say, so the gossip served its purpose and the friend can mock it.

links.note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not left; Kuruntokai 352: the woman says she knew the reality of the small dull evening only when she could not see him.
links.teaches: The couplet states the late discovery of evening's pain as a bare fact, and the poem gives the sign through which she learned it, the creature that leaves its day-tree lonely at dusk, so the knowledge the Kural reports is shown arising from a scene in which the hour itself repeats the parting.

links.note: Both foster mothers ask யாங்கு வல்லுநள்கொல் தானே of a girl who refused milk held up in a fine vessel at home: Akananuru 105 follows the question with the raiders' road of Ezhini's bowmen, Kuruntokai 356 with the scalding muddy water she must gulp.
links.teaches: The shared formula of the refused milk and 'how will she manage' is a stock frame of the foster mother's lament, and the two poems show its slot filled differently: the long poem measures the girl's leaving by the road's dangers, the short one by what she must now drink, so the same frame can carry either fear or tenderness.

links.note: Kural 1261: the woman's fingers are worn from marking the days since he left; Kuruntokai 358: the friend speaks to the woman who scores lines and clings to the wall, and points to the mullai buds as the season he promised.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the counting of days only as the woman's wasting, while the poem lets the friend answer it with a sign outside the wall, the season's buds, so the count the Kural leaves open is closed by the promised season and becomes ground for comfort.

links.note: In Akananuru 26 the wife turns to their son and the husband, saying he too loves the child, embraces her back and weeps; in Kuruntokai 359 the friend tells the bard that the man embraced his son and the son's mother embraced the man's back.
links.teaches: In both reconciliations the son carries the embrace between husband and wife, and with the roles reversed (in one the husband clasps the wife's back, in the other the wife the husband's), so the akam poets made the child the agreed route back into a marriage after estrangement.

links.note: In Akananuru 22 the girl laughs because during the velan's midnight rite her lover slipped past the guards and his embrace cured her; in Kuruntokai 360 the girl, while the velan misreads her sickness, prays that the lover not come at night.
links.teaches: The two girls in the same veri situation take opposite views of the lover's night visit, one as the cure that mocks the rite and the other as a danger worse than the rite's misdiagnosis, so the veri scene could be turned either to triumph or to selfless restraint.

source_issues: kuruntokai:341 line 1, 347 line 1, 351 line 4, 358 line 7 and 359 line 4 are repaired readings from tamilvu.org (flags); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:341: the colophon files the poem under neythal, but the poem names only spring flowers (kuravam, punku) and the man's absence, nothing of the shore; inferred thinai paalai.
kuruntokai:352: the colophon files the poem under paalai, but it has no road or waste, only the evening hour of the waiting woman; inferred thinai mullai.
